title: Walmart, the Great Company That Remade American Society, Has Finally Been Overtaken by Amazon
excerpt: We want to pause over this change, but even more, we want to tell you how it happened.
body:
We want to pause over this change, but even more, we want to tell you how it happened.

On July 25, Amazon released a quarterly earnings report showing strong growth, and its share price shot up, touching US$580 during trading. At that price, Amazon's market capitalization exceeded US$260 billion.

For the retail industry, this was a landmark moment: at least on paper, Amazon had passed Walmart to become the largest retailer in the United States.

Almost everyone knows Walmart. Far fewer know how it grew from nothing into the world's largest company, with annual sales of more than US$480 billion, or why every e-commerce company has studied its business model closely, and why, even as they close in on Walmart and finally pass it, they still speak of it with respect.

Walmart grew up in the America of the 1970s, and it was a good time to grow: the middle class was rising, the consumer society was arriving, and car culture and suburban life opened up new room for retail. But Walmart did more than ride that wave. Its philosophy was simple: low prices every day, saving customers every last cent, plus a sensible expansion plan, would keep the company healthy and make it a profit.

To give customers prices that were almost too low to believe, Walmart negotiated directly with suppliers, and even with manufacturers, using large, steady orders to persuade them to cut costs and squeeze their margins alongside it;

when American manufacturing could no longer support prices that low, Walmart went looking around the world for places where labor was cheaper, and many people in China, Chile and Bangladesh began working for it;

over several decades these methods proved themselves again and again, and people began to use the phrase "the Walmart effect" to describe the company's impact on American society.

![A Walmart store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702161334XWdPuORYoCye3Ejs.jpg-w600)

One example shows how strong the "Walmart effect" was: scholars found that for 1998 to 2001, the years for which data were available, the consumer price index (CPI) calculated by the US government ran 15% above actual prices. An error of more than 10% is enough to lead markets and the Federal Reserve into wrong decisions.

Walmart was not greedy, but the ample demand it and its customers created together sent its revenue and profit soaring: from 1971 to 2006, Walmart's sales grew by more than 30% a year on average, and in its best year profit grew by 119%.

Over the past 10 years, however, Walmart has failed to keep up that pace. Since 2011, its revenue has grown by less than 4% a year on average, and its profit by only about 1%. Its market value has hovered around US$200 billion, and one by one internet companies such as Facebook, Alibaba and Amazon have overtaken it. The company now cuts a rather lonely figure.

![Chart of Walmart's growth](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702161334f1AL5rkUFZWQBpg3.jpg-w600)

![Chart comparing Walmart's market value with internet companies](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201608161442133El2zQw5978DAWcB.jpg-w600)

Why has Walmart declined? One possible reason is that its low-price model and American way of doing business did not travel well to other countries. In China, for example, Walmart opened its first store at almost the same moment that homegrown e-commerce brands were born. But Walmart missed many chances to expand, while Taobao and JD.com grew their influence at astonishing speed.

At home, things have also shifted a little. Americans still shop at Walmart, but when rock-bottom prices matter less than quality of life or more niche choices, an e-commerce platform like Amazon, or a chain like Whole Foods, which sells food as a lifestyle, is a perfectly good alternative.

### How did Walmart reshape American society?

**Price**

In his book *The Wal-Mart Effect*, Charles Fishman works through many sums like this one:

"In 2004, consumers bought US$124 billion worth of food at Walmart. Had they bought that food at other stores, it would have cost US$146 billion, so on food alone Walmart saved shoppers US$22 billion. On the other goods Walmart sells, being just 5% cheaper than competitors saved consumers another US$8 billion. So by a conservative estimate, people saved US$30 billion in 2005 by shopping at Walmart, as if Walmart handed every household US$270 in cash each year."

What Walmart taught consumers was a disruptive way of thinking about price: at any time, Walmart's price stays the same, below the regular price and not far from the sale price. And every year, the same item gets at least another 5% cheaper.

Much of the time this was a numbers game. At other supermarkets, suppliers would run occasional price-cut promotions; at Walmart, they simply spread the year's discount budget evenly over every day and took the matching amount off the price. But the effect was striking. From then on, whenever you saw the same item elsewhere at full price, or even a little below it, you felt the store was robbing you.

![Walmart's everyday low price signage](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702161335yVKuisCUkHMxGaXn.jpg-w600)

It is fair to say that Walmart all but rewrote the pricing rules of American retail.

**Supply and demand**

In its low-price contest with suppliers, Walmart was not content merely to buy. It even tried to use its market power to improve the whole trading system together with them:

Through a data system Walmart built, every supplier could see the sales records of each of its own products at every Walmart store, hour by hour, for the previous two years. Properly analyzed, this detailed database was a great help in lifting sales.

But at times Walmart's buying power was so great that it could bypass every middleman and go straight to upstream factories to have goods made for itself, or find manufacturers willing to produce for less. The first approach eventually grew into even cheaper "private-label products"; the second was a routine way of applying pressure.

To fill orders and cut costs, suppliers often had to rack their brains and even give up part of their own profit. *The Wal-Mart Effect* describes a rather extreme case: to fill a Walmart order far beyond its own capacity, a bicycle company handed the design drawings for four of its bikes to competitors and asked them to help build them.

Once American manufacturers had squeezed costs as far as they could go, only a global approach could meet Walmart's demand for price cuts every year, and so many jobs moved to countries in South America and Asia where labor was cheaper.

Between 1997 and 2002, for example, Walmart's purchases from China doubled to US$12 billion, then grew another 50% over the next two years. In 2004, the Chinese goods Walmart sold in the United States were worth US$18 billion at wholesale, 10% of all American imports from China.

A single company was enough to push a whole country's manufacturing overseas.

**Lifestyle**

From 1970 onward, more Americans lived in the suburbs than in cities, and whether commuting each day or going out for anything at all, they needed a car.

Walmart's dense web of stores made going out to buy things the same experience almost everywhere. In 2005, there was one Walmart for every 78,000 Americans, and 90% of people had a store within 15 miles of home.

And at a time when Americans' appetite for spending was just beginning to grow and varied choices were scarce, Walmart, which sold almost everything, became the obvious place for one-stop shopping.

It was cheap, too. From the lower middle class earning only 30,000 yuan a year to the upper middle class earning close to 100,000 yuan, people grew used to shopping this way. In the late 20th century, this broad American "middle class" made up 70%-80% of the population.

### Why was a giant like Walmart overtaken in the end?

**E-commerce**

"Online commerce will be a very large market, and many companies will profit from it. We are pleased with what we have done so far, and even more excited about what we want to do next." Jeff Bezos wrote these words at the end of his letter to shareholders after Amazon went public in 1997.

In 1994, Bezos started amazon.com in a garage, hoping to overturn the experience of buying books in a store. Twenty years later, Amazon had grown into a global e-commerce giant selling an average of US$240 million worth of goods a day: books, music and video, clothing, household goods, toys... and even computing power in the cloud.

![Amazon](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021613363d1IaGVY6vonh40O.jpg-w600)

In many ways Amazon resembles Walmart. It, too, pushes suppliers to cut costs: when it first went into books, and later when it began selling e-books, it went through similar negotiations with publishers.

It also makes money in a similar way: by raising how much each customer spends and keeping customers loyal. At Walmart, a broad range of goods and rock-bottom prices guarantee a basic level of spending per customer, and stores across the country have taught many people to do one big shop a week. At Amazon, a precise recommendation system makes it hard to resist buying a little more each time, and Prime, the membership service on which Amazon has spent heavily to speed up delivery, gets goods to you within two days, which is no worse than driving out to buy them.

Amazon is not only a retailer but also a technology company. In the earnings report that carried Amazon past Walmart, the biggest highlight was Amazon Web Services (AWS): its growth rate rose from 49% in the first quarter to 81% in the second, making it Amazon's fastest-growing business.

In the first six months of 2015, AWS brought in US$3.39 billion, 7% of Amazon's revenue. But its operating margin was about 17%, far higher than that of the retail business.

![Chart of AWS revenue and growth](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702161336Il6NmcjJOS7Rhz0w.jpg-w600)

This is one reason Wall Street is willing to value Amazon more highly: it is an internet company that does both retail and technology fairly well, and while it is expanding fast, whether it makes money does not matter much yet. That reasoning cannot be applied to Walmart.

**Global expansion**

From 1991, Walmart began exporting its low-price model to other countries, especially to emerging markets where consumer demand was growing faster. International business now makes up 30% of Walmart's revenue, with China, Brazil and Mexico contributing the most.

Brazil and Mexico, both in South America, were among the first overseas markets Walmart entered. In Brazil, Walmart once spent US$764 million to buy more than 140 local supermarkets, department stores and wholesale markets of all sizes, securing its place as the country's third-largest retailer. Its online sales there have also done well, growing twice as fast as the local average.

In China, though, Walmart faced a completely different situation:

In 1996, Walmart opened its first store in Shenzhen's Luohu District, becoming the first foreign retailer to enter China. Nineteen years later it had 412 stores in the country. That is more than rivals such as Carrefour and RT-Mart, but after several rounds of closing old stores and opening new ones, the number fell far short of Walmart's own expectations.

As in other overseas markets such as Germany and Japan, Walmart tried to copy in China the business model and corporate culture it used in the United States, but did not adapt to local shopping habits, and it lost appeal with customers. When it first arrived, Walmart set a sales target of US$100 billion for China, yet even at its peak in 2014 the Chinese market brought in only about US$12 billion.

Walmart was also slow to move into e-commerce. Several years ago China overtook the United States as the world's largest online retail market, and the field is led by Alibaba and JD.com, which built up their B2C (business-to-consumer) retail businesses quickly while Walmart expanded slowly. They now hold 44% and 14% of the market respectively.

Walmart formally launched its own e-commerce strategy in China only in 2011, by taking a controlling stake in Yihaodian. But because of clashes over how to run the business, and because Walmart kept tight control of core lines such as fast-moving consumer goods, Yihaodian's market share has never been satisfactory. Its sales of more than 20 billion yuan in 2014 ranked only seventh in the industry, about one-sixth of JD.com's.

**Diversification**

In the United States, as the distribution of wealth has shifted over the past 10 years, Walmart's customers have changed from the "middle class" in the broad sense to the "lower middle class," who earn less and care more about value for money.

For somewhat better-off American families, price has, in the past two years, stopped being the first thing on their minds as they walk the supermarket aisles, and even traditional retailers now have a chance to beat Walmart. More chains have begun to put their effort into design, fashion, quality, distinctive offerings and the shopping experience. The customers they target are fewer, but their margins are bigger.

![A Whole Foods store](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702161337FQyWcBPlfiEOKkg5.jpg-w600)

A classic example is Whole Foods, the organic supermarket that has taken off in the United States in recent years. It leads America's "new living movement," and the ideals it promotes, a high quality of life, green and healthy food, and care for the environment, all strike a nerve with the American middle class.

What draws customers to Whole Foods is not only its wide array of goods and spacious, comfortable stores but, more importantly, the new way of life it offers and the values its customers share. As for price, that hardly matters: fruit and vegetables at Whole Foods usually cost 1.5 to 2 times what they do at an ordinary supermarket.

Even on low prices, Walmart's greatest strength, retailers such as Dollar General are challenging it. These are America's "dollar stores," and their customers are mostly housewives, who typically go to Walmart once every two weeks and, in between, visit dollar chains for everyday items such as toilet paper or cola.

The financial crisis brought boom times to the dollar-store business, as tens of millions of consumers turned to dollar stores for cheap household necessities. Since the end of 2005, the three dollar chains Dollar General, Family Dollar and Dollar Tree have grown to a combined 25,340 stores, and they have also made it onto the Fortune 500 list of American companies.

Although Amazon has overtaken it in market value, by revenue Walmart is still the largest listed company in the world.
